zh.summary: Fault Line 是一家独立的临床与心理健康 AI 安全研究组织，通过对抗性测试、数据驱动风险分类学（FAULT）和监管合规证据转化，帮助医疗 AI 产品获得监管审查所需的独立安全证据。
zh.judgment: Fault Line 卡在监管真空的结构性位置上——临床 AI 部署速度远超验证方法建设速度，其将评估结果翻译为 ISO 14971 / MDR / FDA 820 合规证据的服务层有望成为行业准入门槛，而非可选增值服务。
zh.replaces: 客户自建安全团队手动运行未经验证的基准测试、临时性红队演练、以及合规部门将随机 AI 行为硬套入 ISO 14971 / MDR 证据框架时的大量人工文档与统计工作。
zh.segment: 临床与心理健康生成式 AI 的独立安全评估、医疗器械合规证据生成、以及面向医疗系统与支付方采购方的第三方验证服务。
zh.product: Fault Line 提供面向临床与心理健康 AI 产品的独立安全评估平台，核心是通过 API 接入客户产品后，运行数千条对抗性对话，覆盖其 FAULT 分类学中 22 个临床风险维度（该分类学由 139 个失效模式经 14,232 条数据因子分析归纳而来）。平台输出每项风险维度的每次对话伤害概率量化指标、针对具体维度的改进建议，以及可直接嵌入 ISO 14971 风险登记册的合规证据包。除平台外，Fault Line 还提供嵌入式评估工程（与客户安全团队共建测试流程）、独立研究合作，以及将评估结果转化为 MDR、FDA 21 CFR 820、NIST AI 600-1 及多州 AI 法案所要求证据格式的服务。Neuly 案例显示，从接入到提交医疗器械注册共耗时 6 周，期间完成 7,500 余条对抗性对话和 22 个维度的测试（公司披露）。
zh.customer: 目标客户分三类：正在部署或迭代临床 AI 产品的公司（需外部独立验证支撑部署决策）、AI 实验室安全研究团队（合作推进前沿临床风险研究）、以及医疗系统和支付方的采购团队（采购前及部署后需独立测试）。痛点频率与模型更新直接绑定：生成式 AI 的随机性意味着每次 prompt 修改、scaffolding 调整或底层模型更换都可能改变安全表现，因此再测试是持续性运营需求而非一次性项目。Neuly 案例中客户强调无法为所有场景编写脚本，说明核心痛点是覆盖未知交互空间（公司披露）。
zh.workflow: 输入为客户产品通过 API 接入 Fault Line 平台；平台运行审计智能体和临床红队人员，针对 FAULT 分类学的 22 个风险维度执行对抗性测试。处理阶段生成量化安全分数（概率乘严重度矩阵）、具体到某风险维度的改进建议，以及 ISO 14971 对齐的风险评分。交付物包括可直接放入医疗器械技术文件的安全证据、变更控制记录，以及支持上市后监测的重复性测试流程。迭代闭环：客户实施改进后，数小时内重新运行相关维度 mini-audit，与固定基线做统计对比（含置信区间），据此决定发布或继续修改（公司披露，Neuly 案例）。
zh.business_model: 定价页未被抓取，具体费用结构、按审计次数计费或订阅模式均未披露。从 Neuly 案例可推断存在项目制交付（6 周医疗器械证据构建）与后续平台持续集成的组合；案例中提到双方同意扩展合作以更紧密地将平台集成到 Neuly 的软件生命周期中，暗示可能存在按年平台使用费或服务费（推断，未经公司确认）。单位经济方面，若平台与分类学可跨多个产品和客户复用，边际成本随审计次数增加而递减；但此假设未有任何已披露数据支撑。
zh.traction: 公司披露：创始团队曾部署服务逾 100 万患者的临床 AI 产品，完成全球首个心理健康 AI 聊天机器人 Class IIa 医疗器械注册，并向 FDA 和 MHRA 提供数字疗法与生成式 AI 监管建议。Neuly 成为首批将生成式 AI 育儿支持工具注册为医疗器械的产品之一（公司披露）。FAULT 分类学论文为 Zenodo 预印本，检索时 907 次浏览、113 次下载。缺失证据：未披露收入、Neuly 之外的具名客户数量、合同金额或 ARR；pre-seed 阶段本身暗示商业化仍处于早期验证期。
zh.moat: 相比通用 LLM 安全工具，Fault Line 的差异化在于数据驱动的 FAULT 分类学（139 个失效模式归纳至 22 个维度）与临床红队人员的组合，以及将评估结果直接翻译为监管合规证据的能力。相比客户自建安全团队，独立性是核心价值——监管框架明确要求独立评估，而创始团队自身有产品方经验，使其了解监管方实际关注什么。壁垒条件：分类学必须随文献和新失效模式持续更新；若监管机构自行编码标准化评估协议，Fault Line 的角色将从定义标准降级为标准内的工具提供商，压缩定价空间。
zh.funding_read: Pre-seed 轮由 Frontline Ventures 和 Concept Ventures 参投，表明投资人认可独立临床 AI 安全评估作为可产品化的服务方向。下一里程碑可能是平台 API 化与 2 至 3 个额外临床 AI 客户签约，以验证经常性收入模型；具体资金用途未在任何检索材料中披露。该轮金额相对于后续平台开发与合规基础设施投入较小，团队大概率需要在 pre-seed 与 seed 之间快速跑通至少一个可复用评估管道并展示管线牵引。
zh.risks: 风险一（监管内化）：若 FDA、MHRA 或 EMA 将标准化临床 AI 评估协议写入法规（如 NIST AI 600-1 实施细则），Fault Line 的证据翻译层可能被监管方自有工具替代，从不可或缺变为可选便利。风险二（模型层替代）：若基础模型提供商内置满足监管要求的安全评估管道并开放给下游应用方，独立第三方测试需求量将显著下降。风险三（分类学漂移）：22 个风险维度基于 132,505 条对话构建；当临床 AI 扩展至多模态、agentic 和跨会话记忆场景，现有维度可能不足以覆盖新失效模式，需持续重算，增加研发负担并削弱最全面的定位。
zh.takeaway: 对创业者的可借鉴做法：将评估结果到监管证据的翻译层作为独立产品出售，而非绑定在某个模型或产品上，类似临床 CRO 骑在制药研发之上。早期以开放预印本形式发布核心分类学（FAULT）建立学术公信力，同时保持商业平台的封闭性，是在定义品类与保留定价权之间的平衡策略。将合规标准（ISO 14971、MDR、FDA 820）直接写入交付物模板，使客户无需二次转换，降低采购摩擦并缩短销售周期。
zh.watch_next: 可验证指标一：Neuly 的医疗器械注册是否被 UK MHRA 或 EU Notified Body 正式批准，这将验证端到端证据链的有效性。指标二：未来 6 个月内是否出现第二个或第三个具名客户（非 Neuly），以判断平台是否可跨产品复用。指标三：Who audits the auditors 框架论文是否进入同行评审期刊；若停留在预印本阶段，学术公信力壁垒可能弱于团队定位所暗示的程度。

en.summary: Fault Line is an independent clinical and wellbeing AI safety research organisation that provides adversarial testing, a data-driven risk taxonomy (FAULT), and regulatory compliance evidence translation to help healthcare AI products obtain the independent safety evidence required for regulatory review.
en.judgment: Fault Line sits at a structural juncture where clinical AI deployment is outpacing the development of validation methods; its evidence-translation layer (converting eval results into ISO 14971 / MDR / FDA 820 artefacts) is poised to become an industry entry gate rather than an optional value-add.
en.replaces: In-house safety teams manually running unvalidated benchmarks, ad-hoc red-team exercises, and the heavy manual documentation and statistical work of fitting stochastic AI behaviour into ISO 14971 / MDR evidence frameworks.
en.segment: Independent safety evaluation, medical-device compliance evidence generation, and third-party validation services for clinical and wellbeing generative AI, targeted at health-system procurement and regulatory submission.
en.product: Fault Line operates an independent safety-evaluation platform for clinical and wellbeing AI products. Core capability: via API, the platform runs thousands of adversarial conversations against its proprietary FAULT taxonomy of 22 clinical risk dimensions (derived from 139 identified failure modes condensed through factor analysis on 14,232 data points). Outputs include per-conversation probability-of-harm scores, targeted improvement recommendations tied to specific risk dimensions, and ISO 14971-aligned evidence packages ready for medical-device technical files. Beyond the platform, Fault Line offers embedded evaluation engineering (working alongside client safety teams), independent research collaborations, and compliance-evidence translation spanning UK/EU MDR, FDA 21 CFR 820, NIST AI 600-1, and emerging US state AI statutes. The Neuly case study documents 7,500+ adversarial conversations and 22-dimension testing completed within a 6-week window from integration to medical-device submission (company-reported).
en.customer: Fault Line addresses three buyer segments: clinical AI product teams needing external independent validation for deployment and release decisions; AI-lab safety teams collaborating on frontier clinical risk research; and procurement teams at health systems and payers requiring independent testing before and during deployment. Pain-point frequency is tied to every model update, prompt edit, scaffolding change, or regulatory resubmission—generative AI stochasticity means re-testing is a recurring operational need, not a one-time project. The Neuly case emphasises that teams could not script all interaction situations themselves, underscoring the core need: coverage of unscripted interaction space at scale (company-reported).
en.workflow: Input: the client's AI product is connected to the Fault Line platform via API. Processing: auditing agents and clinical red-teamers execute targeted adversarial tests across the 22 FAULT risk dimensions, generating quantified safety scores (probability × severity matrices) and named-dimension improvement recommendations. Output: ISO 14971-aligned risk scoring, a safety case for the technical file, change-control documentation, and a repeatable post-market surveillance process. Iteration loop: the client implements fixes, re-runs mini-audits on relevant dimensions within hours, compares against a fixed baseline with confidence intervals, and proceeds to release or further modification (company-reported, Neuly case study).
en.business_model: No pricing page was retrieved; specific fee structures, per-audit pricing, or subscription tiers are undisclosed. The Neuly engagement implies a project-based delivery (6-week medical-device evidence build) plus ongoing platform integration for lifecycle updates; the case notes both parties agreed to expand their work to more tightly integrate the platform into Neuly's software lifecycle process, suggesting a potential recurring service-fee component (inference, not confirmed by the company). Unit economics: if the platform and taxonomy are amortised across multiple products and clients, marginal cost per additional audit or risk-dimension test should decline—but no disclosed data supports this assumption.
en.traction: Company-reported: founders deployed clinical AI serving over 1 million patients, achieved world-first Class IIa medical-device registration for a mental-health AI chatbot, and advised FDA and MHRA on digital-therapy and generative-AI regulation. Neuly became one of the first generative-AI parenting-support tools registered as a medical device (company-reported). The FAULT taxonomy preprint on Zenodo had 907 views and 113 downloads at retrieval time. Missing evidence: no disclosed revenue, no named clients beyond Neuly, no contract values or ARR; the pre-seed stage itself implies commercialisation is still in early validation.
en.moat: Compared to general-purpose LLM safety tooling, Fault Line differentiates through its data-driven FAULT taxonomy (139 failure modes condensed to 22 dimensions) combined with clinical red-teamers, and its ability to translate evaluation results directly into regulatory compliance evidence. Versus client-built internal safety teams, independence is the core value—regulatory frameworks explicitly call for independent evaluation, and the founding team's product-side experience means they understand what regulators actually scrutinise. Moat conditions: the taxonomy must be continuously updated as literature and new failure modes emerge; if regulators codify their own standardised evaluation protocols, Fault Line's role shifts from standard-setter to tool-provider within that standard, compressing pricing power.
en.funding_read: The pre-seed round, co-invested by Frontline Ventures and Concept Ventures, signals investor conviction that independent clinical AI safety evaluation is a productisable service direction. The next milestone is likely platform API-ification and signing 2–3 additional clinical AI clients to validate a recurring-revenue model; specific use of funds is not disclosed in any retrieved material. The round size is small relative to the platform development and compliance infrastructure investment required, so the team will need to demonstrate a reusable evaluation pipeline and pipeline traction between pre-seed and seed.
en.risks: Risk 1 (regulatory internalisation): if FDA, MHRA, or EMA embed standardised clinical AI evaluation protocols into regulation (e.g., NIST AI 600-1 implementation guidance), Fault Line's evidence-translation layer could be replaced by regulator-owned tooling, shifting from indispensable to convenient. Risk 2 (model-layer substitution): if foundation-model providers build and open up regulatory-grade safety evaluation pipelines to downstream application developers, demand for independent third-party testing will decline materially. Risk 3 (taxonomy drift): the 22 risk dimensions are built on 132,505 conversations; as clinical AI expands into multimodal, agentic, and cross-session-memory scenarios, existing dimensions may be insufficient, requiring continuous recomputation and weakening the most comprehensive positioning.
en.takeaway: Actionable practice for entrepreneurs: sell the evaluation-to-regulatory-evidence translation layer as a standalone product rather than bundling it with a specific model or product—analogous to how clinical CROs ride on top of pharma R&D. Publishing the core taxonomy (FAULT) as an open preprint early builds academic credibility while keeping the commercial platform closed, balancing category-definition with pricing-power retention. Baking compliance standards (ISO 14971, MDR, FDA 820) directly into deliverable templates eliminates the client's secondary conversion step, reducing procurement friction and shortening sales cycles.
en.watch_next: Verifiable indicator 1: whether Neuly's medical-device registration is formally approved by UK MHRA or an EU Notified Body, validating the end-to-end evidence chain. Indicator 2: whether a second or third named client (beyond Neuly) appears within 6 months, testing cross-product reusability of the platform. Indicator 3: whether the Who audits the auditors framework paper enters a peer-reviewed journal; if it remains a preprint, the academic-credibility moat may be weaker than the team's positioning implies.

How independent safety testing helped Neuly achieve medical device status — Fault Line Fault Line Approach Research Blog About Book a call Approach Research Blog About Book a call → ← Blog Company 21 October 2026 How independent safety testing helped Neuly achieve medical device status How Fault Line built Neuly's medical device risk register, enabling it to become one of the first generative AI parenting tools registered as a medical device. Ben Carrington Co-CEO Contents At a glance The challenge About Neuly Why Fault Line Building the medical device evidence Optimising product performance & safety quickly Independence that builds confidence What’s next 7,500+ adversarial conversations 22 clinical risk dimensions tested 6 weeks from start to medical device submission At a glance Within two weeks of integrating, Fault Line had built the backbone of Neuly’s medical device risk register by running thousands of adversarial conversations against the world’s most comprehensive clinical AI risk taxonomy . Neuly used the results to strengthen the product before launch and become one of the first generative AI parenting support tools for families of neurodivergent children to be registered as a medical device. The challenge Generative AI is moving into regulated healthcare faster than the methods for proving it is safe. Traditional medical device validation assumes predictable outputs from known inputs. Generative AI breaks this model because it can answer the same question or perform the same task differently each time. Its behaviour and performance can also differ whenever its prompt, scaffolding or underlying model changes. Whilst regulators figure out a path forward, clinical AI companies seeking medical device status face two options: Shoehorn generative AI into traditional risk evaluation, verification & validation and post-market surveillance methodologies that won’t survive regulatory scrutiny. Compensate for the stochasticity by running testing and/or clinical studies at such high sample sizes that the cost and time requirements are untenable and can’t be kept up post-market. Neuly chose a third path: put its AI through medical device aligned independent adversarial testing. That sets a high bar for safety. “We had controls in place to identify and flag risky conversations. What we didn’t have was a way to test how the product behaves at scale before a single parent used it, across situations we couldn’t script ourselves, and a method for turning what we found into concrete improvements. Fault Line gave us both.” — Deepthi Uppala, CTO & Co-Founder, Neuly About Neuly Neuly is an AI coach for parents and carers of neurodivergent children. Through voice and text conversations, it helps families understand their child, work through everyday challenges and build strategies that fit their child’s needs, alongside any professional support the family already has. Neuly remembers each child’s profile across sessions, so its guidance becomes more personal over time. The team behind Neuly has spent years in paediatric ADHD and autism support. Their users are often parents at the end of a long day, worried about a child they love. The company cares deeply about user safety and building a product that keeps parents coming back to it. Why Fault Line Neuly chose to work with Fault Line because the team has been where Neuly is. The founders led the regulatory strategy, clinical AI research and commercial rollout of the world’s first AI mental health chatbot to earn Class IIa medical device status in the UK. That product has since assessed more than 650,000 patients and is used by nearly half of NHS Talking Therapies services. The team knows what regulators ask for, what evidence holds up and where generative AI breaks traditional validation methods. That experience sits alongside more than 34 academic publications and 1,300 citations in clinical AI research, and a decade of shipping production machine learning in healthcare. Fault Line is also at the forefront of how generative AI medical devices will be regulated. Fault Line has turned that experience into a platform for independent, scientifically rigorous evaluation, monitoring and optimisation of clinical AI. Clinical and product teams stress test their AI agents with the most comprehensive clinical AI evaluation platform on the planet , and get back quantified, statistical measures of safety and performance that meet international regulation, governance and compliance standards. The two teams embarked on a partnership to build the safety evidence for Neuly’s medical device registration. Building the medical device evidence Fault Line worked alongside the Neuly team to run a series of medical device grade audits that became the backbone of the product’s risk management and post-market surveillance activities. Integration was quick. Neuly connected its AI to the Fault Line platform via API and the first audit was running the same week, baselining performance through thousands of adversarial conversations, with audit results providing a range of safety measures and risk controls for improving the product’s performance along specific risk dimensions. After the Neuly team implemented those controls, audits were re-run at scale to verify they were effective. The results were translated into ISO 14971 aligned risk scoring so the evidence could slot straight into the technical file without the team having to rework it. Fault Line’s methods and evidence now sit at the heart of the AI safety case in Neuly’s technical file, and Neuly has a repeatable process for keeping that evidence up to date as the product changes over time to support change control, post-market surveillance and ongoing performance monitoring. Updates to a medical device, such as a change of foundation model, can normally mean a lengthy re-evaluation. With the Fault Line platform, Neuly can generate the evidence for a product update within minutes. Optimising product performance & safety quickly For Neuly’s product team, the biggest day-to-day value was speed. The team needed to know quickly whether an edit made the product better or whether the change negatively impacted any specific performance sub-dimensions. A clinical AI product can behave differently across many situations after any change, whether to a prompt, the scaffolding around the model or the model itself. Without a reliable way to measure the effect, it’s a guess which behaviours a change has affected and what testing it needs. This often slows down development, pitting clinical and product teams against each other in a tension between shipping fast and shipping safely. The Fault Line platform turned that into a tight loop. Each audit came with targeted safety improvements tied to the specific risk and performance dimensions they were designed to address, so the team could see exactly what to change and why. The Neuly team could review the improvements and deploy them the same day. Running targeted mini-audits on the relevant risk dimensions then showed within a couple of hours whether the change had worked. Because the platform can also load in product-specific evals and performance classifiers, the Neuly team could also check that an update hadn’t adversely impacted usability or made the product less helpful to the parents using it. That meant Neuly could make several rounds of improvements in a fraction of the time a single round of manual testing would normally take. Every change was measured against the same baseline, so the team could statistically compare versions with confidence intervals directly and move forward with confidence. “Integration was ready within days. The audits came back with specific recommendations tied to named risk dimensions, so we could change the prompt, re-run the relevant tests and see the effect the same day. A quantified score against a fixed baseline took the argument out of release decisions.” — Laura Douglas, Lead AI Engineer, Neuly Independence that builds confidence The independent nature of Fault Line testing gives the Neuly team confidence to ship knowing that every release can be measured and checked against a clinically grounded set of risks that is always up to date with the latest findings, research and publications in clinical AI safety . Beyond the impact on product improvements and medical device evidence, the independence Fault Line provides has also become a useful asset in external commercial, partnership and investor conversations. Independent evaluation against an explainable, scientifically grounded methodology gives those stakeholders a transparent view of how the product performs against clinical risks. “Partners and investors ask the same question: how has this been tested? Pointing to independent adversarial testing against a published clinical risk taxonomy, with a methodology we can explain line by line, is a much stronger answer than describing our own internal checks.” — Deepthi Uppala, CTO & Co-Founder, Neuly What’s next Following the medical device project, Neuly and Fault Line have agreed to expand their work together to more tightly integrate the Fault Line platform into Neuly’s software lifecycle process and build out more materials to support Neuly’s governance, compliance and commercial conversations. Max Planck UCL Centre for Computational Psychiatry and Ageing Research, London, UK Description As large language models are more frequently used for clinical and wellbeing purposes, the regulatory and clinical scrutiny increases, requiring AI manufacturers to provide proof that they tested all possible risks. Current taxonomies and benchmarks are handcrafted by experts, ultimately representing the (subjective) perspective of the authors. As the literature on clinical AI safety grows rapidly, the field has become fragmented and no single taxonomy covers the entire risk space. The field lacks a unified and objective taxonomy that covers the full diversity of potential risks of clinical AI, scales alongside the growing literature, and allows the quantification of sufficient safety testing. We present FAULT (Factor Analytic Unification of Literature Taxonomy), built through a data-driven pipeline characterising clinical AI risks. We produce an automated pipeline summarising the scientific literature, finding 139 unique clinical AI failure modes. We then investigated the co-occurrence of these failure modes across 14,232 health-related real-world and benchmark data using factor analysis, revealing that these failure modes can be condensed into 22 risk dimensions due to overlap in the constructs. Importantly, analysing existing benchmarks with this taxonomy indicates that no individual benchmark covers the full risk spectrum of clinical risks. Finally, we conduct an epidemiological analysis of the prevalence of these risk dimensions across 132,505 benchmark and real-world conversations, illustrating that current benchmarks lack representativeness for clinical risks as it presents in the real-world. Our work provides a novel approach for defining a taxonomy of clinical AI risks in a data-driven way which enables quantification of what sufficient safety testing looks like for clinical AI, and provides a standardised blueprint for future safety benchmarks.
